- When sentiment is bullish (≥0.67) and model shows gradual upward trend, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >+5% from prior day), model tends to overshoot; cap forecast growth to 2–3% per day unless sentiment remains strong.  
- If official supply net is negative and sentiment is bearish, model often underestimates downside; add 1–2% buffer below forecast for 3–5 days.  
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and supply net is negative, model tends to overcorrect; adjust forecast downward by 0.5–1.5% from prior day’s model.  
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows strong upward momentum, check for lagged sentiment spikes — adjust forecast to reflect recent sentiment peaks.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >10% from model, re-evaluate sentiment history for recent bullish/bearish shifts — if sentiment shifted from bearish to bullish, reduce forecast slope.  
- If multiple consecutive days show model underestimating true price (e.g., 3+ days), apply mean reversion: forecast = prior 5-day average + 0.5×(true - model) for next day.  
- When official events are high (≥20 events/30d) and supply net is negative, model often overestimates upside — reduce forecast by 1–3% per event beyond 15.  
- If sentiment is bearish and model forecast is rising, apply “sentiment drag”: subtract 0.2–0.5×(sentiment value) from forecast to reflect market pessimism.
